This is a celebrated work of modernist American poetry, and its fragmented syntax, ellipses, unconventional line breaks, and disjointed dialogue are not errors to be corrected—they are deliberate artistic techniques. Crane uses these devices to:

- Blend the external scene with interior consciousness (Leviathan, Plato, the Rose of Stamboul)

I encountered a lanky fellow on South Street—a restless shark's tooth dangled from his necklace. Through tinted lenses—whether actual green spectacles or merely the tavern's colored lighting—his gaze seemed to glow emerald. He'd drift off mid-conversation, his attention wandering far from where you stood, sometimes seeming miles distant. From the coin-operated piano came the tune "Stamboul Nights," conjuring images as if spun from someone's spent nickel, and he sang along—O Rose of Stamboul, where visions spin like thread! He rambled about sea monsters and the deep, and the liquor made philosophers of us both...

"That's the steamship Ala, bound for Antwerp—remember, kid, wake me at three, she departs on schedule. My sense of time has gone unreliable lately—I keep poor lookout, doze when I shouldn't—" His thin fingers began tapping out a rhythm... "Used to hunt whales, once—I really should straighten out my internal clock—I'm no royalist, I know full well what hour it is—actually, forget it, I'd rather not know—that cursed frozen wasteland up north stole my sense of time entirely..."

O Stamboul Rose—drumbeats spinning tales— "Down in Panama I operated a small locomotive along the Canal—grew weary of that work—then moved to Yucatan peddling household goods and trinkets—ever glimpsed Popocatepetl, that volcanic crater exhaling ash like some voiceless mouth? Eventually I returned to working the shoreline..."

Rose of Stamboul, jewel from the coral depths—fragments of vanished civilizations lingered, teasing at memory—endless corridors of stone worn hollow by water, twisted rock formations—green light—drumming rhythm—all fading into darkness—
outputs.L3:
# The Stranger on South Street

I first saw him beneath the flickering gas lamp where South Street bends toward the harbor, a tall figure whose height seemed almost apologetic, as though he wished to fold himself smaller against the night. His eyes caught me first—green, startlingly green, the color of bottle glass worn smooth by the sea—but they did not quite meet mine. They looked past me, or through me, toward some horizon only he could see, some middle distance where memory and the present hour had become indistinguishable.

He was nervous in the way of a man who has spent too long listening for footsteps behind him. His hands moved restlessly, fingers plucking at his coat sleeve, and when he spoke, his voice carried the peculiar cadence of someone reciting a poem he had only half-memorized, or translating from a language he was still learning to forget.

"Leviathan," he murmured, apropos of nothing, "moves beneath us all, you know. Beneath the pavement, beneath the pilings. We walk on his back and call it earth." He laughed then, a short, private sound, and I could not tell if he was drunk on whiskey or on something less nameable—some intoxication of the spirit that made the solid world seem thin as paper. His philosophy came in fragments, as if he were quoting a book that existed only in his own recollection, its pages scattered and reordered by tide and time.

I asked him his business, his destination, hoping to anchor him—and myself—in something concrete.

"The *Ala*," he said, brightening slightly, though the brightness seemed borrowed. "S.S. *Ala*, bound for Antwerp. I sail tomorrow. Or tonight. Time," he added, almost apologetically, "has never quite fit me, like a coat cut for another man's shoulders. I was a lookout once. A watchman. I learned to count hours by the changing of the light on water, and now clocks confound me entirely."

He spoke then of his life, or what fragments of it he could still summon, as though dredging a net through dark water and pulling up whatever the mesh happened to catch. He had been a whaler once, he said, in seas so cold the harpoon lines froze mid-throw. Later—or was it earlier?—he had run a donkey engine in Panama, feeding coal into its iron belly while the jungle steamed and rotted around him. Yucatán came next in his telling, or perhaps before: peddling goods to villages half-swallowed by ruins, trading tin pots and cloth for silence and suspicion. Each place seemed a station in some private pilgrimage, each departure a small death, a shedding of one more version of himself. Loss seemed to trail him like a wake, and displacement had become, for him, less a condition than a vocation.

Yet through all his wandering speech, one phrase returned again and again, rising and falling like a tide: *"O Stamboul Rose."* He would murmur it and then fall silent, as though the words themselves were a door he could open only partway before it swung shut again. With the phrase came images—ruined cities half-buried in sand, their minarets broken like old teeth; the distant sound of drums, muffled as though heard through fathoms of water; a rose, impossibly red, blooming in some courtyard long since turned to rubble.

I understood, standing there in the gaslight with the harbor smell of salt and tar thick around us, that I was hearing not a man's history but its ruins—fragments of a life he could no longer assemble into a coherent whole, memories that had become myth even to himself. Whatever the *Stamboul Rose* meant to him, whatever city or woman or lost hour it represented, it had become the refrain beneath all his other refrains, the drumbeat beneath the Leviathan's own vast and patient heart.

He straightened his coat, glanced once more toward the harbor as if gauging the tide by instinct alone, and turned to go, murmuring his strange litany one final time before the darkness of South Street took him—tall, green-eyed, and already half a memory himself.
outputs.L4:
# South Street, Late

The nickel piano keeps playing "Stamboul Rose"
though nobody's fed it in an hour—
some trick of the mechanism, some ghost
in the roll that won't let the song end,
and the old man at the bar keeps time
with a finger that trembles like a compass
that's forgotten north.

*Antwerp,* he says, to no one,
to the glass, to the salt-stain
where his elbow's worn the wood smooth.
*Antwerp, or maybe it was—*

He stops. His eyes are the color
of harbor water at dusk, that gray-green
undecided between sky and depth.

*There was a woman.* Always a woman.
*In Panama. Or she had a sister there.
The heat does something to the memory,
melts the edges off the days
so you can't tell Tuesday from a decade.*

The bartender's heard this before,
polishes the same six inches of counter,
doesn't look up. The rose keeps blooming
tinny from the piano's throat,
that Constantinople confection
of a song, all veils and false exoticism,
and it doesn't matter that it's wrong,
that it's Turkish moonlight
sold to sailors as romance—

*Yucatan,* the old man says, correcting nothing,
adding to it. *There were ruins.
Or there was a bar like this one.
I was young. I had a name then
that fit me like a coat.*

He laughs, not bitter, just adrift,
a man who's spent so long
between one port and the next
that he's become the space itself—
no longer sailor, only sailing,
no longer going anywhere
but held here in the amber light,
in the smoke, in the song
that circles like gulls
over water that gives back
no reflection, only motion,

and the rose keeps blooming, keeps blooming,
Stamboul, Antwerp, Yucatan—
all one country now, all one
long coastline of forgetting
where he walks, still walking,
not sure if it's night
or merely evening
in a life that stopped counting
its own hours
somewhere past the last horizon
he can name.
outputs.L5:
# South Street

The old man walked the length of South Street every morning, rain or shine, his cane tapping against the worn cobblestones like a metronome keeping time with memories only he could hear.

His shop had stood on the corner for forty-three years, its faded awning bearing witness to countless changes in the neighborhood around it. New businesses had come and gone—trendy cafes, boutique studios, a bicycle repair shop that lasted less than a year—but his little bookstore remained, stubborn as the man himself.

The people of South Street knew him well. Children waved as they passed on their way to school. Neighbors stopped to chat about the weather, local gossip, or the state of the world. His presence had become as much a fixture of the street as the ancient oak tree that shaded the corner where Fifth met South.

Some mornings, he would pause halfway through his walk, gazing down the street toward the horizon where the buildings gave way to open sky. In those moments, his expression would soften, and those who knew him well understood he was remembering another time—perhaps his youth, perhaps someone he had loved and lost, perhaps simply the countless versions of South Street that had existed before this one.

His story was, in many ways, the story of the street itself: weathered by time, marked by change, yet fundamentally unchanged in spirit. Both had witnessed the ebb and flow of a community's life, absorbing its joys and sorrows into their very foundations.

As evening fell and shadows lengthened across the pavement, he would make his way home, his silhouette merging with the gathering dusk—one more figure in the long history of a street that had seen countless souls come and go, each leaving their own quiet mark before moving on.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a modernist poem in the style of Hart Crane's "Cutty Sark," featuring a fragmented conversation with an old sailor in a waterfront bar.
counterfactuals.output:
**Nightwatch at the Sailor's Rest**

Salt-crusted brass, the bar rail worn
to the sheen of a marlin's flank—
gin going flat in the fog-thick air
and a foghorn somewhere practicing its one word
over and over into the black harbor mouth—

*I shipped on the* Flying Cloud *once*, he says,
*or was it the* Thermopylae*—* 
                                        no matter—
*eighty-nine days Melbourne to the Horn*
*and the sea like a green hand closing—*

                    (the gramophone drools out a torch song,
                    something about Avalon, always Avalon)

—old man, your knuckles are a chart
of every reef you never quite escaped—
                    *Aye. Called her the* Bird of Dawning*.*
                    *Sang timbers all the way from Foochow—*
                    *tea in the hold going bad-sweet, sweet-bad—*
                    *and the mate a devil, and the cook worse—*

The bar-light swings. Somewhere a rope creaks
that is only a door, only a hinge,
only the wind mistaking itself for weather—

*You ever seen St. Elmo's fire, boy?*
                    *Green as a drowned girl's eyes.*
                    *We thought it Judgment. It was only—*

                                        (glass to lip, the amber tips and empties)

*—only voltage. Only the sky
clearing its throat.*

                    Outside: the tankers hum their low
                    unbroken vowel against the pilings,
                    a language older than his, newer than mine.

*Singapore had a whorehouse smelled of frangipani*
*and the Opium den next door smelled of nothing,*
*nothing at all, which is worse—*
                    *I lost a year there. Maybe two.*
                    *Time keeps different watch at anchor.*

He is not narrating. He is only
the sea's leftover syntax,
a hull still ringing after the wave has passed—

                    *We rounded the Cape in a gale that ate the mizzen*
                    *whole, like it was nothing, like it was*
                    *an oyster and we the pearl inside—*

The bartender polishes something already clean.
Dawn is a rumor at the window,
gray and unconfirmed.

*Boy, you still there?*
                    *Boy?*

But I have gone where all his sentences go—
                    out past the breakwater,
                    out past the arc-lit gantries,
                    into the actual dark
                    where the *Cutty Sark* and the *Bird of Dawning*
                    and every ship he ever loved or lied about
                    are running still, canvas cracked full,
                    racing something that has no name,
                    only the old wake widening
                    behind us both, forever,
                    into no port at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness poem mixing overheard dialogue, a jukebox playing "Stamboul Nights," and imagery of ships, whalers, and drowned cities.
counterfactuals.output:
**Salt Static**

the jukebox coughs up *Stamboul Nights* again, brass and sand-colored,
a woman two stools down says *he never once came home smelling right*
and I think of harpoons rusting in attics, of oil rendered from something
that used to sing under the ice—

*—another round, and keep the coins coming, keep her coming, keep her spinning—*

the record hisses like a tide going out over rope and barnacle,
Constantinople dressolves into brine, minarets bending like masts,
someone always says *I heard the city sank whole, bells still ringing down there*
and nobody laughs because the beer is flat and the door keeps swinging open to fog

ships in the wallpaper, ships in the ashtray smoke,
a whaler's jaw bone nailed above the bar like a doorframe to somewhere else,
*he said the water gets thick before it gets deep, thick like memory,*
thick like the horn section looping back to the same four bars forever

*Stamboul Nights, Stamboul Nights*—the needle doesn't skip, it insists,
insists like a drowned bell insists, like a compass insists north
even when north is just more water, more hull, more listing light

the man at the end says *my father went down with the Petrel in '58*
and someone else says *there is no Petrel, there was never a Petrel*
but the bone above the bar creaks anyway, agreeing with no one

I keep hearing coral in the trumpet part,
keep hearing gulls that are actually just chairs scraping,
keep seeing the city under the glass of my drink—
spires, and stalls, and someone selling lanterns to no one,
lanterns that still burn down there, don't ask me how, don't ask
the jukebox, it only knows the one song, it only knows the going down

*—she left on a boat, he says, she just left on a boat—*
and the boat is the bar and the bar is the boat and the record spins
like a screw working loose from the hull of the whole wide night

somewhere the harpooners are still rowing toward something enormous,
somewhere the drowned towers keep their clocks running backward,
somewhere *Stamboul Nights* plays for an audience of barnacles and rust
and I am here, elbows in beer-rings, listening to a woman
half in tears say *he never once came home smelling right*
while the brass horns dip below the waterline
and do not, do not, do not come back up
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a surreal, fragmented poem about meeting a strange old seaman with green eyes who rambles about Panama, the Arctic, and time?
counterfactuals.output:
**The Man Who Sold Me Weather**

He was sitting on the dock where the dock used to be,
green-eyed, salt-cracked, a compass rose
tattooed backwards on his throat—
*north pointing in,* he said, *always in.*

*Panama,* he said. *The canal is a wound
that never closes. I watched them cut the isthmus
like a wrist. Ships came through
wearing both oceans on their hulls.*

He smelled of copper coins and rot,
of something that had once been fruit.

Then, without moving his mouth,
he was somewhere colder—

*Ice doesn't melt,* he said, *it remembers.
I have seen a walrus with my grandfather's face.
I have watched the pole spin loose
like a doorknob nobody fixed.*

His hands were maps.
His knuckles were the Azores.
When he opened his palm
a whole harbor tipped out, tiny, sinking.

*Time,* he said—and here his green eyes
went the color of drowned bottles—
*time is a rope with no one holding either end.
I have coiled it. I have coiled it wrong.
Every knot's a year I lost in Colón,
every year's a knot I tied in Baffin Bay.*

I asked him his name.

He became, briefly, a gull.
He became, briefly, the smell before rain.
He said: *I was never young. I was only
early for my own disappearing.*

The tide came in without water.
The dock that wasn't there, wasn't there more.

I have his green eyes now,
somewhere behind my own—

two small drowned harbors,
still sinking,
still counting the ships.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of experimental poetry that blends broken syntax, refrains like "O Stamboul Rose," and imagery of coral, ruins, and the sea, evoking Hart Crane's style.
counterfactuals.output:
# O Stamboul Rose

O Stamboul Rose — the coral keeps
what drowning gave it: syntax
of the salt, unfinished —

*bone-white minarets lean into*
*what the tide will not forgive*

I saw — no, syntax fails me here — the sea
had eaten half the alphabet of noon
and spat the rest in shells, in

O Stamboul Rose, your ruined
architecture of the tongue, your
towers built from what the water un-

remembers. Coral is
a slow refusal. Ruins
are the sea's

grammar, broken
into archipelagos of sense —

*and still the gulls stitch nothing*
*into nothing, bright*

O Stamboul Rose — I could not
say you whole. The minarets keep
falling into what they mean,

the coral keeps its architecture
of undoing, and the ships —
their hulls unspeaking, in the swell —

carry the drowned vowels
home, or nowhere, O

Stamboul Rose, the sea
does not conclude. It only

opens, closes, opens —
what the ruin knows, what coral
knows: that beauty is

the wreckage
learning how to sing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic monologue in fragmented free verse where an old sailor recounts his travels—Antwerp, Yucatan, the Arctic—interspersed with musical refrains and dreamlike imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**Salt-Tongue: A Sailor's Refrain**

*(sing it low, like fog through rigging)*

I was young once—
                              or the sea told me so,
told me in Antwerp
where the bells
                    hung heavy as drowned men's coats
and the canals
             wrote their own scripture
in oil-slick and gull-cry.

*Down, down, where the anchor sleeps,*
*down where the drowned keep their promises.*

There was a woman there.
There is always a woman there.
Her hands smelled of cardamom and rope-tar.
She said *stay*
                    and I heard *storm*
                                        (the ear does what it wants
                                        after forty years of gale).

—

Yucatán came after,
                    or before,
time folds like a wet sail
                    in memory's hold.

Green there. God, the green.
Jungle breathing like something
                    that hadn't finished being born.
Limestone wells
             where the Maya dropped their gold
                    and their girls
                                and their prayers
             down into the blue-black throat of the world.

*Down, down, where the anchor sleeps,*
*down where the drowned keep their promises.*

I drank something in a hut with no walls—
                    fermented, fire-lit, forbidden—
and dreamed my ship
                    had turtle shells for a hull
and the stars
             navigated *themselves*
                                                into new configurations
                    just to confuse me.

—

Then ice.
God's own iron country.

The Arctic doesn't speak.
It *withholds.*
Light for six months,
             dark for six more,
                    and somewhere in between
             a silence so complete
                                you could hear your own blood
                                             deciding whether to keep going.

I saw a whale there once—
                    or the ghost of one,
                                        white as the unwritten page,
             breaching through ice-fog
                    like a cathedral deciding to walk.

*Down, down, where the anchor sleeps,*
*down where the drowned keep their promises.*

—

Now I am an old man
             with salt in the creases of my knuckles
                    and no ship
             but the one that sails
                                        nightly
                    through the leaking hull of sleep.

Antwerp, Yucatán, the white unbearable North—
             they are not places anymore.
They are *songs*
             my body still remembers
                    how to hum.

Somewhere, I am still nineteen
             and diving
                    into water that has no bottom,
                                only more
                                        and more
                                                    blue.

*Down, down, where the anchor sleeps.*
*Down where the drowned—*

                                                    *(the old man trails off,*
                                                    *hums the rest,*
                                                    *closes his salt-crusted eyes.)*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
